canDo: Can recognise and use the present participle, the gérondif and verbal adjectives in texts and discussions about food and health, expressing simultaneity, manner and condition in tighter sentences.
review: Review day 15’s nominalisation and journalistic style and day 13’s passive/impersonal structures: compress “qui + verb” relative clauses into present participles, and rewrite “quand/si/parce que” clauses as en + -ant.
input: Read: an analysis of ultra-processed foods, an opinion piece against “moralising about food” and a reader’s letter about a vegetarian canteen — mark every -ant form and decide whether it is a present participle, a gérondif or a verbal adjective; listen: a nutritionist on “eating lunch in front of a screen”, a consumer segment on “healthy” snacks and a news flash on “vegetable boxes on prescription” — note the advice and figures as you listen.
output: Write: a ≥220-word opinion forum post on a “junk food tax”, with at least 3 gérondifs or present participles; speak: a 4-minute monologue on “banning food advertising aimed at children”, then respond in the debate to the examiner’s doubts about “reimbursing dietary advice”.
checkpoint: Reading and listening accuracy ≥80%; can tell fatigant/fatiguant and convaincant/convainquant apart; forum post ≥220 words with at least 3 correct -ant structures; a 4-minute monologue without breaking off.
challenge: Today’s challenge: find a news item on RFI’s « Journal en français facile » or TV5MONDE about food, nutrition or health, and write your opinion in 3 sentences with a gérondif (e.g. « En lisant cet article, j’ai compris que… »), or record a 1-minute spoken response.

questions.why: The text explains in turn the definition, research findings, an experiment and experts’ advice — an article that takes stock (faire le point). It doesn’t single out companies for blame (A goes too far), nor recommend specific recipes (C has no basis).

The text says: « plus la liste des ingrédients est longue et incompréhensible, plus le produit a de chances d’appartenir à cette catégorie ». The text says explicitly that it is “not just ready meals” (ruling out B); price is only mentioned as an attraction in the first paragraph, not as a way to identify them (ruling out A).

The text says: « une corrélation ne prouve pas une causalité ». The text says the findings are « convergents » (consistent), ruling out B; the studies followed « des dizaines de milliers de personnes », ruling out C.

The text says: « se consomment plus vite, si bien que la sensation de satiété arrive trop tard ». Both menus had « les mêmes quantités de sucre, de sel et de fibres », ruling out A; taste preferences aren’t mentioned, ruling out C.
The context « les soirs de fatigue » shows it is a stopgap for tired evenings (dépanner = to help out in a pinch). B and C are unrelated to the context.

The text says: « c’est l’offre elle-même […] qu’il faudrait faire évoluer », recommending more cooking from raw ingredients. They explicitly reject a full ban (« répondent par la négative », ruling out A) and oppose making families feel guilty (ruling out B).

The concluding paragraph: « Je plaide donc pour une approche plus apaisée ». The author grants that information « reste indispensable », ruling out B; the apps that score meals are exactly what she criticises, ruling out C.
The text says: « non pas parce qu’ils mangent mal, mais parce qu’ils ont peur de mal manger ». A and C are exactly the reasons the author rejects.

She concedes first, « Je ne nie évidemment pas les enjeux de santé publique », then, with « Mais », criticises turning every meal into a “moral test”. A is the opposite of the text; chocolate is only used as a comparison, not presented as healthy (B is wrong).
The text says: « c’est ignorer les contraintes bien réelles qui pèsent sur elle ». The author doesn’t judge organic food itself (B), and the single mother is just an example (C).
assumer = to accept without guilt, in contrast with the earlier « craquages » (giving in to cravings). A means the opposite; C isn’t in the text.
The opening « Ayant lu dans vos colonnes la lettre de M. Garnier » shows this is a reader replying to another letter, signed by an individual — not a town-hall notice or an investigative report.
The text says: « Contrairement à ce qu’il affirme, nos enfants ne vont pas « manquer de protéines » ». Price and meat quality aren’t Mr Garnier’s arguments.
« qui boudait les lentilles, en redemande depuis qu’elles sont servies en curry »: prepared well, children enjoy it. A is the opposite of the example; C overgeneralises.
The text says: « la commune a pu acheter des produits locaux de meilleure qualité ». Dairy products are still on the menu (second paragraph), and the number of meals isn’t mentioned.
« Je comprends qu’on soit attaché à ses habitudes », plus an invitation to come and taste — a mild tone, open to dialogue. There is no contempt, nor pessimism.
The presenter opens with « déjeuner devant son ordinateur », and the doctor then discusses the effects and gives advice. Working hours and dieting aren’t the topic.
« Il enregistre mal ce que l’on avale […] une heure plus tard, on a de nouveau faim ». It doesn’t say people eat more slowly (A) or digest better (C).
« certains ont même l’impression qu’en quittant leur bureau à midi, ils seraient mal vus ». Neither the distance to the canteen nor saving money is mentioned.
« la sensation de satiété met une vingtaine de minutes à s’installer »: slowing down lets the feeling of fullness arrive in time. B is a separate piece of advice about eating with colleagues.
« couper la messagerie interne pendant quarante-cinq minutes à l’heure du déjeuner ». “midi et deux” refers to the slot in which other companies ban meetings, not to a longer lunch break (C).
« il ne s’agit pas de culpabiliser ceux qui mangent un sandwich devant leur écran de temps en temps […] Ce qui compte, c’est l’habitude ». He considers the company’s role “essentiel”, ruling out A.
The segment compares labels and finds that “healthy” products don’t live up to their name (« Pas toujours »). It doesn’t recommend brands or give recipes.
« J’ai comparé une quinzaine de produits en lisant les étiquettes » (a gérondif expressing manner).
« aussi grasses et aussi salées que les chips de pommes de terre », the opposite of A; production costs aren’t mentioned.
vendeur as an adjective = catchy, good for sales. The speaker means the nutritional value is about the same; only the name sells better.
« les personnes souffrant de diabète ou de surpoids et disposant de faibles revenus » (two present participles defining who is eligible).

V16-01.exZh: Screens take up a large place in teenagers’ lives.

V16-07.exZh: On busy evenings, frozen meals remain a quick fix.

V16-13.exZh: To pay the rent, she holds down two part-time jobs.

V16-14.exZh: For some sociologists, what’s in the shopping basket is a marker of social status.

V16-15.exZh: Local authorities can change what canteens offer by buying more fresh produce.

V16-16.exZh: This farmer’s testimony offers another perspective on the question.

V16-17.exZh: The gratin was such a hit that the children ask for it every week.

V16-18.exZh: Changing your diet overnight is no small thing.

V16-20.exZh: In this company, leaving before 7 p.m. is frowned upon.

V16-21.exZh: Remember to take a break every two hours.

V16-22.exZh: Many shoppers feel they have a clear conscience when they buy organic.

title: Participles, the gérondif and verbal adjectives
